neg.tekst: Let me start by saying that this game is awesome, I love the idea of an Idle game that you can leave on the side or bottom of your screen, it functions well. The pixel art and animations are great, the idea of an Idle Farming Simulator is a dope idea in general and I think for the most part this game has been executed well. However, at this point in time I cannot give it a positive review because at only 22 hours into the game I had already completed it. As someone that has played a good amount of Idle games I was pretty confused at this point. It had me questioning if that was truly it and I was kind of stumped, no more content, I'm just expected to restart a new farm? I've never played an Idle game that's taken this little of time to complete. After completion there's not much to do apart from watch your money go up and collect poop to fertilise crops. So it's kinda left me feeling like I've paid for SOME decent hours of Idle game play, but after that I'm pretty much just dealing with a quarter of an animated wallpaper that sits on my screen... I tried looking for a road map for the game because I was genuinely confused due to its shortness, however I couldn't find anything. I'd love to see more content being rolled out for the game in the near future and I'll make sure to keep an eye out to delete my review if this game does receive updates. For now though it does more or less feel like the end product is an animated wallpaper and that the game maybe should be in Early Access, however at the end of the day this is just my opinion.

Some overwhelmingly positive games on steam make sense, some don't. This is definitely one of the later. That said, the game is fine. If you want a game to sit in the background while you do other stuff, then it's great for that. The biggest issue is that over a couple of days and 4 or 5 hours of active playtime at most, you've done everything there is to do. You've unlocked everything, built everything, done it all. You have maps left to unlock but that's just different scenery - you build the same things, in the same order and unlock the same stuff, in the same order with nothing new whatsoever. There's nothing incremental, no new game+ system, nothing at all you would expect in current idle games. If you want a pixel art style game to run in the background for a couple of days before you move on. you could do a lot worse. If you want an idle game that will last longer than a few days, you could do a lot better. /edit Quite a few silly sausages have felt the need to leave comments on 70+ hours playtime and how it must be amazing value because of that. To be clear, I left the game open for ~3 days - it's an idle game. Actual time interacting with the game was maybe 4 or 5 hours at most, half of that was on different maps to see if anything else opens up - it turns out it doesn't. Even leaving it running overnight has no real benefit, there's no point having more money or more flowers or anything - there's nothing to do with any of it.

Game is pretty much completely done after 3 days, which is very short for an idle game. Game systems abruptly end and have nothing else to do so no more progression (nothing to do with all your money, nothing to do with excess collected poop, etc.). I only left it running for the achievements. No appeal to start a new farm (new farms just have obstacles to make your life harder but since there's no end-game progression then it's just simply new farms to make your life harder).

Generally well designed for what it is, but I can't in good conscience recommend it to friends I love or care about without substantial disclaimers. The "you can leave this running in the background and focus on your other work" ethos would be better served if its design included some form of direct encouragement or reward for _not_ looking at, mouse hovering to inspect/scroll through it, or clicking on it for at least N minutes of duration at a time (without encouraging poking at it every N+1 minutes, either). As-is, I straightforwardly 100%-ed the achievements within an unhealthily game-obsessive, otherwise-unproductive time period, short in duration relative to the game's likely design expectation, but unhelpfully long relative to other life responsibilities. Has a toggle-able option to try to slow the pace of production in an attempt to disincentivize staring incessantly at it, but ultimately that feels more like a self-punishment than an effective focus aid or play deterrent, hence my design suggestion. [Edit after release of Winter update] I'm seeing other reviewers critiquing how the new update added a lot of RNG grind trying to get good upgrades out of the newly-added NPC and having to check it every 12 minutes. Coincidentally enough, using the "focus mode" toggle I mentioned above not only halves crop production time, it also doubles that new NPC's cooldown timer...which ever so happens to make the duration close-enough to identical to the oft-recommended 25 minutes of focus spans for Pomodoro timers. I'll see if I can treat the distracting addictiveness of this game's design with a little more self-control and may flip my review to positive to acknowledge the designer's making good-faith efforts and being generous with substantially-additive free DLC.
Once you choose a farm layout, you can't change it. Once you place animals, you can't remove them. 5+ achievements require you to make multiple saves, starting from the beginning multiple times.
I like the concept and quality, But there is too little content. No depth at all.

The new update adds a bunch of grind that reduce the enjoyment of the game. The new chip system has no respect for you time with a 12 minute cooldown no mater if you reroll of buy everything available, with no way to upgrade the number of available chips or reduce the time. You now have to check on the game every 12 minutes if you want to progress. Also, the fact that you can't remove animals or certain buildings from the farm once they are placed also goes against the original feel of the game of carefree farming, now you miss click or do an achievement and your stuck with stuff you don't want.

It's a nice game but not worth overwhelmingly positive, once you unlock Splunk and have the ability to replant, the game plays itself. The progression is very linear, not really interesting choices to be made. I decided to 100% the game and the animal and 250k harvests achievement took way too long, even when the farm is fully optimised. After 24h you have kind of seen everything in the game, and then it is just waiting for unlocks/achievements.

It's a bit too involved for a lot of the game for my idle game tastes. You can't fully automate until you unlock the final resident. Up until that point you need to manually plant at fairly frequent intervals since crops get picked pretty quickly. The game is also a bit too big on the screen to just let it run in front of any other window.
It seems like it can be fun. However the layout of this game is aggravating. Without a windowed mode I can not recommend this.

I love getting addicted to casual/idle games so was excited to pick this up because of the outstanding reviews. Unfortunately I was pretty disappointed. All too often lately a game that describes itself as "relaxing" is just a red-flag for it not having much meaningful content. In Rusty's Retirement, you buy a plot of land then plant seeds on it. Your robots will water and harvest the crops but can't plant them, so you need to check back every few minutes to plant more for them. After what seems like an eternity you have enough cash to buy another plot of land, which... you can plant more seeds on. This is literally the entire game. I don't know what the other reviewers are smoking. The top review talks about "optimising carrot production yields" and "redesigning the farm so his bots don't get stuck on trees". None of this is present in the game. If you want more carrots you buy more land and plant more carrots. The only tree you can place is a Christmas tree, and your bots clip right through them - pathfinding is not a consideration at all in this game. Were these reviews bought? The main goal of the game is to unlock more crop types, which you can do by harvesting a certain amount of other crops. I was excited when I unlocked the bot who sold decorations because that sounded like actual gameplay, but then I realised my goal is currently to harvest 300 cauliflower (and I have 20 similar goals after that). Why would I waste valuable crop space on decorations that do nothing? Plenty of other games have decorations give area buffs so the player can justify being creative with them BTW. I'll admit the 'sitting at the bottom of the screen' gimmick appealed to me at the start too, but after an hour or two I realised it was just that - a gimmick. If I'm working on something, what's the difference between having it on my screen, on my second monitor, or just in the background until I want to tab over to it? If anything, having it on the screen is just way more distracting. I found myself glancing at it constantly to see if there was something to do, and the answer was usually yes - three squares need replanting.

Progression is too front loaded. Fun and lots to do at first but quickly runs of out depth 10 hours into play (or should I say idling? which means actual play time is much shorter). Extra maps are not exciting enough to repeat the same exact gameplay over again. Lots of free idle games out there have better longevity than this one.

Honestly, super disappointed with this game. You very quickly hit the point where resources dont matter and you've unlocked all the mechanics. A vast majority of the time is just waiting for the next crop to unlock. Theres no real long term progression which is really unfortunate. The game was super neat when every little while you got a new bot with more mechanics, but after a very short period of time (just a few hours) you have all the bots and you have all the mechanics. I know its a game where the main mechanic is waiting around, but ive played other desktop buddies that have much more of a sense of progression. If you're looking for a desktop buddy thats at least somewhat engaging, id pass on this one.

Only option is very tiny sliver of the screen where you cant read or see anything or 50% off your screen is taken up so you cant do anything else. Needs more zoom options because it is unplayable. Having to manually adjust all other windows to fit this game is more hassle than its worth.

Very poor support for MacOS. Moving it to a different screen makes it disappear and become unusable. It seems to really struggle if you move it to a screen with a different resolution. After many months of waiting for a fix, literally nothing has come out.

I wish there was a "Meh" neutral rating on Steam. The game is cute and all but it lacks "intent"/scaling depth and progression. It's easier and faster to skip everything to unlock all the parts of the map. It only takes a few hours to see everything. Hell it's even more pleasant to play without all the buildings in place, like I hate that I can't disable Splunk. It should be balanced to have some incentives to explore most options of the game. The deserts maps are probably the most interesting as you have to really think about your output. Apart from that some bugs: - Sometimes your workers will get stuck, the only way to fix it is to reload the save. - Some maps unlock when you haven't finished the previous one. - Actually it's good because I couldn't finish that one because I couldn't buy the map parts. The button never shows up even though I click on the button. (Edit: this was not a bug, I just didn't have the money but there was no visual clue to notify me) - You can build on some map parts you didn't buy/demolished (eg: The blossom forest) - You can't shift elements, it should allow us to move them even if some parts are overlapping on the old placement. - Some UX is confusing, like the bulldozer icon next to the big red X. Does the red X destroy elements/saves or is it the bulldozer? It's ok when you think about it but the user shouldn't have to think about it. For a very simple IDLE game, the performances are quite AWFUL even at minimum performances :/ Like if you want to stream it on Twitch and do something like a Geoguessr it is unplayable (even worse if you Chroma key it, don't try that just cut the top) It seems to be a full screen window? Maybe if you make the window just the size of the game and remove most of the pass through clicks it would help?
Gets repetitive extremely fast, not very fun and requires a lot more attention than an afk game should

Yeah honestly, the negative reviews here are right. It's definitely cute and I like the format (bottom/side of the screen). However it's so repetitive, there's not enough space to do things, it really does idle at a higher CPU than I'd prefer, and it requires constant coddling. The price increase seems steep, and by the time you get to the point where you can actually start exploring the higher seed types or the livestock etc. you run out of land to do it. After the first one and a half farms I gave up on it. I regret spending as much as I did on it.

Less of a game and more of interactive wall paper. If you go into this looking for an idle game this really isn't much of a game. IF you go into this trying to optimize production structures there really isn't that type of game. And to my knowledge there isn't an endgame or goal. Basically treat it like background music and something to occasionally look at and its kind of interesting. If you're looking for an actual game I'd look else where.

Game is alright, but it will lag your PC all around unless you fiddle with the settings(and this is while I have a 4090). So it sort of defeats the purpose of being an AFK game. So I don't really like having this on while working. Great idea and amazing pixel art though.

Was expecting more out of a "Overwhelmingly Positive" reviewed game. Is the novelty of sitting at the bottom of the screen inflating the score? There are free idle games with far more inventive and involved gameplay to try out there like Famers vs. Potatoes idle. Rusty's Retirement isn't terrible, but it just doesn't offer much. Plant some veggies, unlock a new one ever 5 minutes. Repeat 40 times with nothing too interesting happening and then it's over. No prestige, no advanced finances. If you're looking to get a casual gamer into idle games, I could see this being a good buy, but if you're looking for a deep idle game worthy of a price tag, this isn't it.
Unfortunately very little depth. I left it running over night, and was essentially out of new things to do immediately after. If it were free I'd be disappointed I wasted my time downloading it.

I would like to bring in some nuance to the overly positive reviews. I guess the bar is pretty low with this genre. Don't get me wrong this is a decent enough idler for the price and it was even fun for the first few hours but it gets boring pretty quickly as there just isn't that much content to it. After I had unlocked all the crops I was basically just leaving it running solely for the achievements but wasn't having fun with it, and now I don't see myself playing it again. I do like that once you've unlocked everything it can become fully automated, but since there isn't really an endgame to play towards it feels kinda pointless. This lack of content would be acceptable if it weren't also for the issue of optimization. For some reason the game's power usage is through the roof even after lowering the settings. For a pîxel art game that is supposed to run in the background while multi-tasking, this is surprising and a deal-breaker for me.

Nothing to this game at all really. Set everything up, then wait...a lot. I don't see an overwhelmingly positive in this at all, not even a positive. Just another electricity waste. Also, it takes up enough resources to slow your entire machine down. I'm running it on an I9-12900K with 64GB of DDR5 and a 3090ti. It makes Steam, Chrome, and everything else very sluggish.

Rusty's Retirement is addictive but not particularly fun. The styling is cute and the concept of a game that takes only a small portion of the screen is really novel, but I can't shake the feeling that there's just nothing to really do. The game is absurdly slow but not quite slow enough to have dissuaded me from watching over the farm and making small modifications for hour-long stretches. I never finished a farm and felt exactly satisfied - it always feels like there's something more to do but no real reason to do it. All of this probably sounds absurd coming from someone with 300+ hours in the game, but consider that the vast majority of those hours were completely unsupervised. I maybe spent 10 hours actually engaging with the game. This is because very early on I found that leaving the game to run overnight is by far the most fun way to play; when you come back, there's much more to do, since you'll have vast piles of money and biofuel. These are the few fleeting moments where Rusty's Retirement feels like a game. Perhaps this is all expected for an idle game and the real mistake was me playing it in the first place. I thought it would be a cute little diorama to have running on the bottom part of my screen but it ended up being so distracting that I decided to quickly complete all the achievements just to be done with the game. No matter how I look at Rusty's Retirement, it isn't a game I'd recommend. If you have time to play a game, there are plenty that are more engaging and intricately designed. Rusty's Retirement is just here to waste your time.

I tried to like this game, but there just isn't enough here. Very little interaction with the world. Planting seeds gets boring pretty quickly. Why do my radishes keep vanishing? I can't recommend this to others. It's cheap, so if you want to try it, 🤷

I just lost nearly 3 hours of progress. Even though the game is supposed to have an autosave feature, it failed to work, and my save file has reverted to the first 5 minutes of play. I can't find my recent data anywhere.

Very meh game. Doesn't do enough, it's really just slow for the sake of being slow so you do other things in the meanwhile. Plant seeds, upgrade your bots, plant more seeds, only 2-3 actual "house" upgrades that don't do much. The genre has potential but this ain't it.
Pretty boring even for an idle game

the concept of the game is great, but after spending a few days grinding for achievements it just felt empty. i got most of them but stopped at placing 10 cows and pigs on a single farm. Theirs only 1 NPC in the game that digs for fossils ( which you need to get more animals ) and he's so slow it would take me DAYS of doing literally nothing letting the game run in the background while i do other things to achieve it. and while theirs nothing wrong with that, it just doesn't feel very accomplishing to achieve something for doing nothing but wait. you'll reach the end of the game within your first day or 2 and at that point you just start again on a new farm or watch your money go up for the achievements. if you need something to do at all times its pretty good for that, but otherwise i cant really recommend it knowing how short the game is.

It was "alright" But it annoys me that you have to restart/create a new save file everytime they have new contents/collaborations. I made a mistake by adding the "automatic replating" feature which you cant turn off at all, and it becomes boring so-very-fast. You dont have to do anything. Literally nothing. Just open the game and let it run in the background to generate money which you can use to buy decorations, etc etc, forever and ever. They also wont allow you to remove farm animals once you have them. Annoying, simply annoying.

Its a charming lil game, wish it could be played in a window but well. unfortunately the performance issues on any resolution I have higher than 1080 are abit too problematic. so for me I can't recommend this, unless you have 1080 or lower resolution, which is a shame as it is a cute lil game but the lagging my computer is a deal breaker.
Neat but, don't recommend. finished over 2 days with ~ 1-2 hours of interaction

This really seems like a game I would enjoy, but playing this on Linux is just completely unenjoyable due to the game's lack of a transparent window via Proton and the black void that fills the entirety of the game's window as a result. At the very least give us some kind of default sky image to select rather than having Rusty live in the shadow realm.

The tedium of constantly having to check, replant, check, replant, any time a crop is done growing and being harvested really makes this, just not an idle game. The industry seems to not understand the idler genre anymore. Idlers, are, in essence, something that idles. It just accumulates, as you do nothing yourself. That's the concept of an idler. I can't even recommend this because of the amount of micromanaging you have to do. It's not an idler.

If cute and cozy and a cheap price tag is all it takes for you to like a game, you'll probably find joy in this game. There's just not enough meat on the bones of this game to keep me interested. The gameplay loop strikes immediately and it just becomes a game of "wait until you can afford the next tier of items, plant those, repeat". To its credit, it's an idler that requires more user input from most to get things done, but a lot of it is still automated. It took around 6-7 hours to explore the vast majority of the content without going after each little individual achievement. It's just not what I was hoping for. I was hoping for more varied content and hoping it'd lean more into a farming sim than an idler.

Solid "OK out of 10". I like the premise. Fun little time waster, but many of the mechanics will have you wondering "Why?". It's not exactly balanced in terms of progression, the last and most expensive upgrade? The ability to automatically replant crops. Oh, and he'll only do that when the entire plot is empty. Those big 4x4 plots? Yeah, gonna have to wait for each of the plants to fully harvest before they're useful again. The animal ranches are completely pointless also. They will use the lowest value crop, but what if you are between harvests? That's right, it'll use the expensive crops. Oh, and your biofuel converters? You can't select which crops to use so expect them to use up all your cheap crops. Want to get rid of the ranches? You can't. They're a building and can't be destroyed, And the bots for automation? You don't unlock the bot upgrade till halfway through so you'll probably be wasting space placing too many to deal with that. This is the most active I've ever seen an "idle" or "automation" game, because you'll be micro-ing until you can unlock the 4k fuel 20k coin building for automation, then leave the game on overnight and move to the next farm in the morning. There's no point keeping a farm running other than achievements. "Why?"

ive played roblox idle games with more progression then this, how did i get to "end game" progression in 2 days, now im just waiting for crops and sitting doing NOTHING. artstyle is cute though but its a BIG pass

Instead it is a straightforward game of dull progression and limited expansion, it’s an addicting process with unsatisfying results. It's meant to be a calming experience filled with visual beauty but overall it's a low participation activity rather than a game. While the game gets virtually harder you don't get any content in return.
feels too slow and too manual

looks great, but its so slow to get started.. also this isnt a retirement, its a full time job

Sadly the scaling is awful and you can reach the end game within 24 hours pretty easily. Comparing this game to free idle/incremental games, Rusty's retirement does not stack up in terms of content. The best thing it has going for it is the pixel art, which is quite nice. I would recommend this game if you are interested in a simple and quick idle game with nice pixel art, but unfortunately I would prefer a game with a bit more going on. If the developer made the art, then I will check out future instalments with the hope of something more ambitious. As it stands however, Rusty's Retirement is a surface level game with little to do or accomplish.
Looks like a nice enough game but it does not work properly on Linux (runs on a black window, no overlay possible, kinda defeats the concept...). Would have preferred to know that before buying.
After about 15 hours you have seen all the content and there is not much more to do. You can unlock the rest of the achievements but all that involves is just a bunch of waiting, not much else.

Not being able to autoplant seeds ruins the idle automation feel. Sure there's a upgrade for it but that's the very last upgrade. I was hoping to just leave the game on to progress but I'd have to keep checking to see if my seeds are depleted. It's automated for however long the seeds last for and then you have to buy and setup all the plants you need again, usually 5-10 minutes. Also, until you get more bots to gather biofuel and better crops, be ready to jitterclick the golden bell for gold for hours or download a autoclicker. Otherwise progress will feel nonexistent early game.

I wanted to love this game. I thought it could be a side game I leave on while I play other games. But whenever I have it on, my PC lags so much after a while that even switching tabs is in slow motion.

Not a true idler game. It cannot just sit alone and do its thing while you do other things. You have to keep an eye on the game and plant crops, where you make active decisions in the game. Better just buy Ropuka's Island folks. In that game, Ropuka cuts the grass, and you doing anything beyond just opening the game and letting him loose is optional.
Unable to opt out of events.

Rusty's Retirement has a lot of potential, but it probably shouldn't be considered a proper game yet. The visuals are some nice pixel art fitting for the bottom-of-the-screen auxillary Tamagotchi-like experience it is designed to invoke. There is some pleasant background music to be enjoyed here. However, as weird as it sounds, the game would be better without any sound whatsoever. Any incremental savvy person should understand that these games are not meant to be played attentively. Therefore, any sound or music is mere distraction. The best games in the genre, like NGU Idle or Antimatter Dimensions, know that well and come absolutely silent. Worse still that sound isnt't easily toggled while claching with the core idea of the game - to sit at the bottom of your screen. The game has no plot or lore AFAIK. Some postapocalyptic future may be infered, judging by tha fact that all sentient characters are robots and all animals are reconstructed from fossils. The main premise of robots growing veggies to be converted into biofuel is very cute. The gameplay is the weakest part. Core mechanics are nice, but at this point, the game has one, maybe two days worth of content. You play one map to unlock 95% of the achievements, then quickly play two more maps that actually act like fun challenge modes - but then it all just ends. You unlock three more maps, but there is no point playing them. Furthermore, the game is riddled with questionable game design decisions. You cannot sell some of the buildings even if they are detrimental for you. There are fossils that you slowly accumulate with no means to boost their production. Those are used to create animals that probably enhance your production a bit but are not worth the effort. There is honey collection that leads to nowhere. If I ever needed to replay a map, I would rather use my land for actual crops. Worst of all, the game reqires A LOT of micromanagement. Like, you have to manually plant every single crop. Seriously? Rusty cannot plant the crops itself? Automatic seed planting is treated like some endgame option. That is not how idle games work. Overall, Rusty's Retirement works as a nice proof of concept and has a lot of potential, but it needs at least 10x the content to justify the price. I appreciate the effort put into making this product, but selling this for money is kinda insulting to the better incremental games out there. Final score: 5,8
A sad follow up to Haiku the robot. I don't really understand the point of the game. Not for me.

It is well made but... it is a bad game. Even for an idle game there is not enough content, after just 3 hours, I have unlocked most things and idk what else to do now other than starting a new farm. The only thing you really do is planting, there is no real optimization or any meaningful decisions. Get wallpaper engine with an relaxing wallpaper instead, this is basically what it is.
Rusty, I want to love you, you seem like a perfectly nice robot, but please, PLEASE, stop putting wheat in the biofuel generator. I have so many other crops you could use!
Cute but overall pretty boring.

bought this game on a rec from a friend but its very broken on mac. I saw that the developer pulled the swap monitor option last year for mac and never added it back. really sad cause i was stoked to play this, but am gonna refund and hope this gets fixed.

Cute aesthetic but very shallow gameplay. After one day of running it in the background and occasionally tending to it, I've basically done all there is to do - which is, arrange a crop and bots layout and leave it running - and all that's left is to grind different crops (which only vary in how much time and water they need) to unlock other crops, and then completely restart on slightly different maps and do the same thing again. The berries, bees, and butterflies are similarly shallow and don't interact with the normal crops at all. Ranching at least provides fertilizer, but even then it's just "place some robots around and forget about it". No Linux support is a bummer - while it "runs" with Proton, the transparency doesn't work and so you end up with a black background. You can finagle options with winecfg to give it a virtual desktop that doesn't take your entire screen, but it's not as charming when it's not transparent.

+ Chill idle farming game + Can play at the bottom or side of the screen + Cute graphics, chill music. - No post-game content. - Upgrading bots can be a horrible experience, especially if you have a lot of them. Need hotkeys for upgrading them. - Bots, characters seems to do task non-systematic, for example, water bot is watering plant on one crop then switch to another crop without finishing the current crop. - Beekeeping is bad. Berry bushes take a lot of time to yield and need to have Forbic's house first, which is expensive and can't afford at early game. Bee buildings are also very expensive. - All of husbandry is just for farming faster, nothing more. - Because of beekeeping and husbandry is expensive, you can't do anything except farming in early game. This makes the game get boring very fast.

Even for five bucks, this plays like a free-to-play mobile game that someone slapped a price tag on and forgot to adapt for PC. For a game that is supposed to sit at the bottom of your screen while you work, the sheer amount of babysitting, clicking, and basic UI failures makes it completely miss the point of being an idle game. First off, the UI is atrocious. You can't click on an existing building to see what it is, what it's called, or what it actually does. When you're starting out and half the structures look identical, you're left guessing or digging through outside guides just to figure out what you placed. There is zero bulk management. If you need to clear out an area, have fun clicking the demolish tool individually on every single tile. Planting trellis crops like grapes is the exact same nightmare: you have to click the button for every single piece because there is no click-and-drag or brush placement tool. The worst part is the permanent design traps. You can build Animal Feeders, the game does warns you that they are completely permanent and cannot be demolished. I built five or six of them expecting the poop recycling to be a massive progression boost. It's completely worthless. The fertilizer yield is garbage, it takes up a massive amount of horizontal screen space, and now those dead plots are permanently stuck on my screen because the dev decided players shouldn't be allowed to delete them. The automation is completely broken as well. The automated planter (Splunk) moves so ridiculously slow that he might as well not exist. Three-quarters of my farm sits completely empty and unplanted waiting on him, which stalls the rest of the bots and forces you right back into manually planting seeds yourself. On top of that, the market arbitrarily caps your sales at 999 items at a time. When your late-game farm is pushing thousands of crops, you have to sit there spamming menus over and over just to clear inventory. When I have to constantly micromanage basic tasks, fight a clunky mobile interface, and babysit manual sales, it stops being an idle game and just becomes a carpal tunnel simulator. Skip it.

This game is great as an idler and I've used it in the last few days to take small breaks until I discovered that the game progress is not linear : you are forced to make your farm in X "scene", farm it until you unlock the other scene and then lose all your progress to start the new scene and so on until you unlock the last one. That means that also the farming/grinding for the achievements it's unnecessary long because you will end up without things to do while waiting for the last two achievements. What's the point of a limited progress for an idle game? I don't understand all the praise for this game.

Rusty's Retirement is a breath of fresh air for the idler and automation genre, much like how Vampire Survivors shook things up for bullet heaven games. It stands out by doing its own thing, mixing a super satisfying sense of progression with creative mechanics that keep you hooked. Automating your farm, upgrading bots, and leveling up tools is so addictive it is hard to put down. You can already tell this game is going to inspire a bunch of copycats in the future. What really makes it shine is how it works for different types of players. Whether you like to set it up and let it run in the background or you prefer to stay hands-on, constantly tweaking and optimizing, the game makes both approaches feel fun and rewarding. It is accessible to pretty much anyone, no matter how you want to play. That said, there are some oddities and room for improvement. For example, when you get a giant-sized produce, you apparently have to remove the plot entirely or it becomes locked, which feels clunky and unintuitive. Similarly, plots can be locked if the planted crop and the crop sign don’t match, which adds unnecessary frustration. Some quality-of-life updates could make this game even better. Little tweaks, like letting you swap multiple plots to a new crop or clear several plants at once, would save so much time and hassle. It would also be really cool if players could jump in and handle some of the tasks the bots usually do, like watering or building. That kind of hands-on option would make the whole experience feel a lot more interactive and engaging. Being able to switch the farm layout from vertical to horizontal would add a lot more flexibility and make planning feel less restrictive. Even with these little quirks, Rusty's Retirement is a total gem. It is already a standout in the genre, and with a few tweaks, it could easily become a classic. If automation games or idlers are your thing, you definitely do not want to miss this one.

I got Rusty's Retirement from a Humble Bundle. I’ve always had an affinity for desktop games. Games like Catz and Dogz on Windows 98 and the old LucasArts desktop games like Yoda's Adventures are ones I played a lot. I love games that integrate with Windows itself. Rusty's Retirement is such a game. You can run it in the background while doing other things, like watching movies, working, or even playing other games. However, some games aren’t very compatible with Rusty's and may run a bit slower. Especially older MMO games didn’t like it much when I ran Rusty's alongside them. Fortunately, you can alleviate this by setting the game to low-power mode in the settings and turning off focus mode. The game looks fine. The sprite work is decent, and Rusty himself looks nice. However, the design of a couple of the bots isn’t that great. I didn’t like the look of Echo when I first planted his house, but he quickly blended in with the farm, and I don’t notice him that much anymore. I understand the developer took some characters from his first game, Haiku, the Robot (or maybe all of them, I didn’t play that game). The music is also fine. It gives a nice, cozy feeling. However, I turned it off when I started multitasking, so I played 95% of this game on mute. That might be a shame because, from what I heard, the music is decent and very chill to listen to. The achievements are, as you might guess for a partly "AFK" game, a bit of a grind to get. Especially the animal achievements, because getting all those fossils to buy them takes a long time. I understand why this is the case since you need to pad your game out a little bit. I didn’t mind, though, because the game is "fun" in its own quirky way. The game has a couple of different maps you can unlock, each with a unique play style. The desert was my favorite because of the drying-out mechanic. You unlock these maps by opening up all available spaces on the other maps. If you really want to get to a specific map, that’s the only thing you need to do. The game is a nice, chill experience. If you like farm sims, this game is worth the price. I hope the developer keeps listening to the discussion board because there are some quality-of-life ideas there that could make the game better. I will continue to follow this developer, and I hope they make other games in the future. I also plan to pick up Haiku in the near future. Here are a few tips when you start this game: Every house you can build is a literal game changer, though the order you build them will impact your game. If you want to get all achievements, start by building the Reaper’s Outpost with the very first crops. You can then upgrade every crop when you get the new ones. This will make it much easier to gather every upgrade for every crop. Don’t sleep on Forbic. The bushes are useful for getting biofuel fast, and you don’t need to plant many to get going. Don’t forget the butterflies next to them. Remove old bushes with newer ones if you need the space. The same goes for Slate. Fertilization helps a lot with growing crops. However, unless you need the achievements, you don’t need to build that many farms. One with six animals is enough to fertilize a full farm. Splunk, the most expensive bot you can get, allows you to automate the game fully. If you want to run your game overnight or while at work like I did, get Splunk as soon as possible. Unless you want to make your farm beautiful, be mindful of farm spacing. You can position them so one bot can manage nine large farm patches. If you upgrade the gathering and watering bots to the max, they can keep up with the farms. However, this isn’t guaranteed on every map. The desert and winter maps are different, but you’ll find out for yourself.

I think a good idle, especially one you can't actually influence in any regard outside of upgrades, requires a balance between two things above all else. Time between upgrades and, most importantly, the tangibility of your upgrades. This game does not have either. Between when I started playing and now, nothing seems to have actually improved. It feels like no progress has been made. The only difference now is the color of my grass, not truly the rate at which it gets cut. It takes me 6 minutes to upgrade my grass cutting from 2 to 2.1. An increase so minuscule will hardly aid the speed at which I gain any other upgrades, many of which cost double that as is. It's very dissatisfying to see. It doesn't make those lights go off in my brain for having unlocked/earned something, nor does it reward me for investing the extra time to unlock something more costly. It's all so meager that it really doesn't matter at all what you get. It is simply a cute, but unrewarding idle. It feels like the type of game meant to be left on while you're entirely away from your PC, not while you're actively using it. If a very slow burn is your speed, this will likely do just fine for you. If you want upgrades to feel impactful, especially after several hours, then this is not for you.

I think my current playtime speaks volumes for how much I enjoy this little game, but I'll ramble on. Ropuka's Idle Island is a very very simple and basic idle game that sits anywhere on your desktop. It's very easy to resize Ropuka and his island and relocate it so that it won't get in the way of anything, and you can toggle it so that it can or can't take priority over other windows (sit on top). You can also turn off the music and ambience separately, meaning that I can mute the music but still keep the sounds of wind and birds to a "low hum" for relaxation. I've seen some people deem this game "boring", and I get that. This is no action game, there isn't much you can do with Ropuka other than customise him and his island. But it's important to remember this game is intended to give you a little desktop friend who does his own thing whilst you also do your own thing. I personally like big numbers and seeing them rise, so I like leaving him for a few hours and coming back to see millions of grass trimmings. Plus, this game is very low-demand so you can easily run a different game or other programs alongside it! Overall, I love the little chill vibes this game brings. And I love little Ropuka, too.

Games are gentle confessions we make to ourselves: that sometimes the deepest meaning emerges not from epic quests or grand narratives, but from watching something small and diligent go about its quiet business while we pretend to be productive adults. Ropuka's Idle Island embraces this truth with pure, unpretentious charm. It’s less a game and more a living desktop companion—a tiny frog in a straw hat who spends his days peacefully cutting grass, napping in the sun, and slowly turning his little patch of paradise into something uniquely yours. You place Ropuka’s island anywhere on your screen like a playable sticker. While you answer emails, grind spreadsheets, or zone out to another tab, he keeps working. Grass grows, he harvests, resources trickle in. Spend them on better scythes, richer soil, new plants, cozy buildings, or absurd little hats that make your amphibian friend look even more content with existence. The loop is minimalist and meditative: check in occasionally, rearrange a few decorations, watch him wave good morning or settle in for a nap, then let him carry on. Progress feels gentle rather than frantic—no overwhelming pressure, just the quiet satisfaction of watching something grow without you. The dark humor lies in the honesty of it all. Here we are, allegedly evolved creatures, paying money to watch a cartoon frog perform the most mundane task imaginable while we scroll through the same endless feeds that make us feel hollow. Yet there’s something profoundly philosophical in that repetition. Ropuka doesn’t question his purpose. He cuts grass. He improves his tools. He decorates his home. In his simple dedication he mirrors the best and worst of us—the need to tend something, to see incremental beauty emerge from routine, to find peace in the small ritual while the larger chaos of life rages outside the window. The art is genuinely soul-soothing—clean, colorful, and full of those tiny delightful animations that make you smile without meaning to. The island evolves with your choices, and the chill soundtrack (or nature sounds) makes the whole thing feel like a pocket of calm you can summon at will. Some will call it “just a fancy screensaver.” They’re not wrong. But that’s the irreverent genius: sometimes the highest form of interactive art is the one that asks almost nothing of you except the willingness to let something small and wholesome exist in your periphery. Ropuka's Idle Island never pretends to be more than its adorable little ritual. It just hands you a diligent frog, a patch of grass, and the quiet invitation to watch something thrive while you try (and mostly fail) to do the same. In a noisy world that demands constant attention, this tiny island whispers the radical idea that sometimes doing very little, together, is enough. 10/10 would let the frog cut another patch tomorrow. Tiny Pasture, cute "idle" screen game that has turned out to be more of a chore than I thought I was in for. I don't think I'd be being honest if I truly tried to call this game an idle one. The initial few days had me quite hooked, clicking clicking, dragging, coin collecting, saving up. I think I spent a genuine 4ish hours on the first night trying to unlock as much as I could, it was easy stuff and pretty cute to boot. Then you get your midgame setup working well, you have an automatic feeder, cleaner and coin collector that you can upgrade as you wish. I left my game open for maybe 5 hours while I went out to run errands and came back to a pasture full of very sick and hungry animals that had generated very little coin in my absence, despite having the auto-helpers activated. Since then I make sure to come back and check the animals every 1-2 hours at the minimum. You can't even drop food en masse before you leave because food items left on the ground will poof after a certain amount of time has passed , I can't work out the logic behind that decision during development especially since you are paying coins for the food in the first place. Towards end game things are just getting grindy beyond a joke. I unlocked pandas way before deer, zombies, even capybaras I think. And pandas are the only things worth rearing for coins. An important mechanic of the game is the Mystery Curtain used for breeding, but the real benefits of this are not explained in game and I had to find answers in the discussion boards- breeding animals combines their coin drops and can upgrade their rank to a certain point. Had this been even alluded to in the description I would have utilised it much earlier, and since the devs moved the goalposts on the "Lots of animals" achievement I don't think getting that one is possible without knowing this information. Despite this, the maths works out that I'll probably have to leave the game open another 40 hours or so from this point, just to get that final achievement. All while staring down a paddock of 33 pandas instead of the mix of animals the game encourages you to play with. If you don't care for achievements at all and really just want a cute little decorative idle on your screen then maybe this game is for you, although actually unlocking the animals you want will force you to play some grinding regardless. If you like to box things off and finish them properly I'd give this game a hard swerve, if only for that final achievement that unnecessarily triples (or more) the time you'll have to spend playing it to achieve. EDIT- Gave up. Downloaded Gastly mod from the workshop. Maxed out on Rainbow Gastlys and turned several more days grinding into a couple of hours. And I suggest you all do this too.

Overall I think this is a fun and cute game for what it is. As a lifelong lover of tamagotchi and other virtual pets this checks a lot of boxes for what I look for in virtual pet games. There's a decent variety of creatures to pick from and most of them have very cute variants. Currently I have two cats and a corgi that look almost exactly like my cats and corgi IRL which is very fun. The game is a touch slow, but I honestly don't find the progression that bad. It is an idle game, after all. It's meant to be ran in the background for long periods of time. It isn't a game that's meant to be challenging or complicated. It's supposed to be cute and silly, and that's exactly what it is. - All the animals are very, very cute. There isn't a single one I don't like. Even the Zombie is cute, and I was skeptical when I first saw it as an option. The collector in me also very much enjoys all the variations most creatures have, though I would like to see more options in the future. Most animals have five variants, but some only have two, and the Capybara and Panda only have one. Even still, they're very cute and I enjoy watching them run around. - Every animal is bought as a baby and will eventually grow into an adult. But one thing I LOVE is that you can change an animal back to its baby appearance at any time. This lets me have more variation in my pens and lets me choose the designs I prefer. In my case it also allows me to better mimic my real life pets, as one of my cats is very small, so the virtual version can be small too. Very simple detail but it is something I really like. - Food drain is nicely balanced, for the most part. One thing that makes or breaks a virtual pet for me is how often it needs to be fed. Too often and they just die, too slow and you forget about them. If you opt out of automated feeding I find that feeding your pets feels good and isn't punishing. If you want to be more involved in caring for them it is an option. - Overall the game seems decently optimized. I have an OK PC, but nothing super high end. The game is able to run in the background with no issue. I can even play other games or render animations with this running in the background with little no no performance loss. With that said, I can't speak for everybody on performance. I'm not sure how this would run on a laptop or anything else. Still, it is nice to be able to have this open and running all the time, especially with it being an idle game. I have a fully upgraded pen that is filled with animals, decorations, crops, etc and even then it runs smoothly. While I do reccommend this game to anyone who wants cute little animals running around on their screen, it still has a few features that could be better. These aren't things that make the game unplayable for me, I can look past them and enjoy the game anyways, but they might be downsides for others so I'll list them. - There seems to be no point in having multiple pens. Anything that automates the game (auto feeding your pets or auto cleaning the poops) can only be placed in one pen at a time. This leaves any animal in any other pen to starve and get sick. With that said, I am unsure if time passes in other pens if you aren't in them. Even then, if you want to have another pen running in the background you have to swap over all the automated items yourself, and if time doesn't move for inactive pens you aren't earning money from them which makes them even more pointless. - The game runs fairly smoothly overall, but if you have the game open and turn on another monitor (in my case I have an art tablet that acts as a second screen) the game freaks out. If you have multiple monitors it is best to have them all on before starting the game, otherwise it causes massive lag. You ARE able to easily swap the screen the game is running on if you have multiple monitors, which is nice. There's a chance the problem here is with my art tablet and not with the game, so keep that in mind. - The breeding system seems to delete creatures. I do not know if this is intentional or not, but if it is, it is a feature I don't care for. Breeding two creatures deletes both parents and leaves you with a single baby. At the very least you do have the option to inherate the parent's colour/variant/earnings rate. There's nothing in any of the in game tutorials that explains why this might be happening (that I could find) - Animals often get in the way of UI elements and there is no easy way to move them. If you are growing crops and an animal is in front of them the animal will block you from interacting and harvesting the crop. You can click and drag your mouse to make the animal follow your cursor, but they tend to move very slowly. It would be nice to be able to pick up an animal via click and drag to make managing them better Again, overall I would reccomend this game. It is cute and silly. Things I consider "cons" aren't enough to make me not want to play. Not only that, but my cons might simply be a misunderstanding on my part. I haven't been playing long enough to fully 100% know the ins and outs of the mechanics.

Sadly, Steam doesn’t allow reviews to be marked as “Mixed”, which is exactly how I feel about this game. On one hand, if you just want something adorable running in the background, it’s perfect — I’d absolutely recommend it for casual players. On the other hand, if you’re like me — a perfectionist who loves chasing achievements and 100% completing games — then be warned: it’s going to be a long and frustrating journey. The game itself is an idle game, and I genuinely enjoyed it a lot at first. The art is cute, the atmosphere is relaxing, and for a while, working toward achievements felt rewarding. I made steady progress and had fun… until I hit the very last achievement. I’ve earned 54 out of 55 achievements, but “Lots of Animals” is on a completely different level. The final pasture slots are ridiculously expensive — I’ve been struggling with this for three weeks now since earning achievement 54. In that time, with the game running all day, every day, I’ve only managed to afford 2–3 more slots, and I still have 3 left to buy. The next one alone costs 2.4 billion coins. I can’t even imagine what the final two are going to cost. The grind just doesn’t feel balanced. At this point, I’d even consider spending money (if there was such and option) just to buy coins and finally get it over with, which really kills the fun. Don’t get me wrong — the game is adorable and a great idle background experience. But for achievement hunters like me, the final stretch feels like an unreasonable wall, turning what was once a joyful game into a frustrating grind.

In Tiny Pasture to unlock things fast you can make your pets follow you to win money (Rusty has a similar trick with clicking). Well they combined the "cute idle game on the bottom of your screen" with "cute creatures to collect" and that makes it perfect in my eyes. Also you can resize the window and move it around the screen so that's a real plus on my side.

neg.tekst: The game is pretty fun until you reach the endgame, where none of the rarest items seem to drop. I bought this game with a few friends, and we've been farming the endgame for several days now. None of us has found anything beyond Ancient Legendary. The game was fun until we finished it and realized that the last two rarities seem to exist mainly for a handful of lucky players to find and potentially sell for a few bucks on the Steam Market. If you're okay with either purchasing your gear with real money or simply calling it quits after killing the final boss on the hardest difficulties, you'll probably have a good time. For me, though, having two of the rarest item tiers effectively locked behind an absurdly low drop rate makes the endgame feel unrewarding.

To be frank, this game doesn't value your time or your wallet . And I bet you're saying, "Well, duh, it's an idle game. You just let it idle while you do something else. And it's cheap! What are you talking about." Well, let's get into it. In other idle games the gameplay loop is pretty straight forward. The start of the game is very manual action heavy, requiring your almost constant attention, and slowly, over the course of hours or days, the game automates itself into the background of your life to the point that the game basically plays itself. The enjoyment of it is getting to that point in progression where the numbers get big and the amount of effort is minimal. ... Deskrawler doesn't really get there? The issue with the game comes down to its premise- it's an ARPG . ARPGs live or die by loot drops. If loot drops are garbage, you get release day Diablo 3. If loot drops are rare, but build defining, you get Diablo 2. If loot drops are plentiful and awesome, you get the original Borderlands. You see where I'm going here- the more unique, the more diverse, the more plentiful the loot, the more enjoyable the game becomes. Right now this game is very very first day of release Diablo 3. Loot is rare, terrible, and generally just long stat sticks with nothing of value to them besides bigger number = better. It's frustrating. Your entire progression becomes loot focused to the point that you could be several levels above the enemies you're fighting just because your gear isn't good enough to fight things at your level. And, you will end up at a higher level than enemies. You eventually unlock the ability to get hours worth of progress when the game is closed, but this only applies to getting gold and experience. Gold doesn't actually do anything in this game. You can't buy loot with it; instead, you use it, primarily, to upgrade the gear you have (and I'm talking like 0.1 more attack speed or 1% more damage per upgrade) or buy meta passives (like 10% more experience, item find, etc, etc). Eventually you will get to the point that you're just idling to find loot to progress- and loot is very very rare. But, remember when I said this game was like Diablo 3 on release day? The comparison is more apt than you think. Just like Diablo 3 at release, this game also has a real money auction house. You can buy stuff with actual money. Because drop rates are so low, even in the offline mode where you can't use the auction house, it creates this very Diablo 3 predatory real money auction house dynamic. I didn't know about this until I started writing this review. I had been playing offline where the drop rate is so bad that I thought that I must have been doing something wrong. Nope. I wasn't. The game is designed this way. Even with my meta item find passives maxed out, finding decent gear takes hours. And, again, this is the way the game is designed. It's meant to push you towards online mode, which still has terrible drop rates, in the chance that you use the real money auction house. Because, guess what, the developers get a 10% cut of all those real money market transactions. It directly benefits the developer to have low drop rates to funnel people into, basically, microtransactions- which aren't actually that micro when you see that items are selling for $20+. The thing that really chaps me about this? When I played the demo during Next Fest, the item drops were way higher. This tells me that the developers have intentionally bombed item drop rates in all modes purely to get that sweet revenue cut from the market place. It behooves the developer's pockets to have rarer item drops. Sadly, this ruins the player experience to the point that I don't think anyone should purchase this game... Because this isn't a game- it's glorified crypto. You idle for the off chance of finding an item you can sell on the market. The only person this benefits is the developer who both designed the system and gets a cut of those transactions. So, yeah, the game doesn't respect your time or your money or you . Don't buy this game. Don't support this nonsense.

Idle games transitioning from the early game push to the mid game stalling and into the end game grind is a hard path to tread properly. Some games abruptly hit a torturous grind so quickly that you just throw your hands up and uninstall because, well, this is the number go up game. Number not going up. I am effectively locked out of what passes for endgame content because nothing drops. "Oh, you're being hyperbolic," you say. No. I hit the endgame grind, in which gear of three more rarities begin dropping, and haven't seen a single piece in a week of straight farming. I haven't even gotten the legendary reins from the map I've been farming. Things just don't drop. At all. I've had this game running for 300 hours, how have I not gotten a drop at all. It doesn't actually take all that long to hit endgame. Online play chases best times and leaderboards for specific maps. There is no point in doing so because the top people all shilled out $100 on the Steam marketplace to get a full set of the best items anyone's gotten to drop while you're lucky if you've seen a piece, and to be honest, it kinda feels like you'll have a better experience with this game if you sell whatever you manage to get to drop so you can at least make your money back on this game. Which, fun fact, gives the developer money. Huh, a game I respected for not having microtransactions has microtransactions. Can you feel the negative Sims interaction icon over my head through my typing? I'm no stranger to grindy games. I love me a bit of Dragon Quest 9, where it takes 45 hours to hit the end of the game and a thousand to properly finish it in its entirety. The post mid-game loop is rushing grotto map chests to farm that rare 2% treasure chest good item drop chance just so you can fail a 5% chance success rate on the item you're making and get to do it all over again. This is after you've spent hundreds of hours farming your levels enough that you can even get a decent map with decent treasure chests. You can get so granular in that game's farming that you can farm stat point increasing consumables, one at a time, to increase all your party to 999 stats, 1-3 points at a time. There was at least a line of progression in both of these. You felt like your time wasn't being disrespected outright, what with all the other things you got out of the chests and the slow drip of the stat point consumables. And this game has... farming one mission, over and over again, so you can farm the rifts, and get nothing from either of them. Neat. I'm remembering why I never seriously considered Diablo. Check back in a year or two. Either the devs will give this more time or they won't.

I wrote a whole thing about how it took three weeks for me to realize exactly what was wrong with this game, but it got long and boring so here's the moderately shorter version: It feels cheap and poorly put together. The weapon model rendered on your character frequently looks nothing like the inventory icon, all of the inventory/store/etc. screens are clunky and awkward and seem to have no discernible logic to how they behave, and some of the UI/UX design decisions are so mindbogglingly terrible they are actually kind of funny (eg, hovering over your health potion to prepare to drink one causes a tooltip popup that BLOCKS YOUR HEALTH ORB). The itemization is so boring and uninspired it's actually kind of impressive. The only "exciting" drops are Divine gear and set runes; everything has almost entirely randomized stats and will be useless 95%+ of the time. So even if you know you want that Serrated Greatsword of Agony, seeing one drop is completely unremarkable because the odds of it actually being worth using are vanishingly small. The game almost seems like it's going for the launch D3 route, where the good stuff is so rare people will be driven to the RMAH to buy it and the devs can take a cut - which is a ridiculous system to have in an idle game. The final straw for me was when I found an item that was objectively better than what I had in every metric, and when I equipped it my dps fell by over 40%. Either the damage calculations are bugged, or they are so arcane and convoluted that that was intended behavior; in either case, the primary purpose of an idle game is to make interesting decisions and then let them play out in real time (with some random events sprinkled in as rewards); if the decisions I make have turned out to be mostly arbitrary, I don't see any reason to keep playing.

If I remember correctly from the demo, there were 2 more abilities for the warrior class. They are gone now. - Stash size was lowered from 80 to 50 slots. As for the map nodes and talent tree nodes, they had icons with padlock. If you hovered your mouse cursor over them, a popup would show up, informing you that this will unlock in the full version of the game. As it turns out, it didn't unlock, it's just gone. Where did the game from the demo go? Generally speaking either the demo was a scam, that was suggesting the full game had more content, than it realy did, or wrong (early) version of the game was released as full release by mistake. Then again there is also a third option: the dev made such great changes to the full release compared to the demo, that it only made such an impression on me, but until the dev says something about it officially, then we won't really know. Considering how much different was the offer from the demo compared to the full release it leads me to conclude, that the demo was falsely advertising the abundance of content in this game. This is another one of those reviews where I wish I could give a "kinda" score, instead of a binary yes/no. The positives; I enjoy the core gameplay loop - it's quite satisfying tabbing back into the game after a few hours to a full inventory to sort, salvage, and stash for later use or future characters. I think ARPGs (where grinding for gear is a core aspect) and idle games (where the grinding is automated) match up fabulously. There's a reasonable (but not exceptional) amount of build diversity (typically each character can be played in 3-4 different ways), and I like that minions let you fill in gaps in your gear while also helping your other characters with progression. And while the balance between characters was bad at launch, the devs seem responsive and are already starting to address that, which is nice. For the negatives; first and foremost, the game has an RMT auction house that operates through Steam Marketplace. I fundamentally dislike schemes like this in games for reasons that should be obvious. Related to this is the absurdly low drop rate for chase minions/gear/runes (because you're supposed to buy them), and the leaderboard conveniently accessible from your inventory, where you can look at all the people who bought their way to the top before you could even think about getting there. The pacing of the game in general is also rough - sometime around level 20 you'll start outlevelling content but still being unable to progress because your gear is so bad, forcing you to grind the highest level stage for hours until prog-worthy gear drops, but by the time you get to level 50-55 you're suddenly tearing through stages with ease, and unable to actually equip any gear that drops because your level is too low (i.e. you're able to farm the level 68 boss at level 55, meaning any gear that drops will have to be put aside for several real life days). Finally, the neutrals; there's no plot, lore, or dialogue at all. You get a paragraph of text when you create a character, and another paragraph of text when you beat the final boss. There's something to be said for a game that cuts to the chase and lets you get right on with killing things, but if you care about that stuff you'll be left wanting. The game will also expect you to play multiple characters (they gain gold for your main even while you're not playing them) which is fine for me but the busywork might not appeal to some. In short; "maybe". The review is negative because if my opinion was placed on a set of scales it would weigh slightly towards negative, but not by much. I'm going to continue playing it because I'm generally enjoying it, but I love both ARPGs and idle games so the game is almost tailor-made for me. I hope the devs continue to support it in future and address the pain points in progression (unfortunately I expect the RMT is here to stay). For now it's a barely-negative, but it wouldn't take much to turn this game into a barely-positive. And for a game that costs a little over a fiver, that's good enough for me.

I assumed that it would eventually evolve into needing to plan a truly coherent, synergistic build to be able to go toe-to-toe with the later stages of the campaign and Nightmare/Inferno. After around level 50 when I had a few legendaries that synergised well, I absolutely dumpstered through the rest of the normal campaign to 70. I went from struggling to kill the level 25 boss at level 30, to wiping the floor with the final level 70 boss at level 57. So from that point, all I had to do from 57-70 is grind the same level. I got excited when I hit 70 and unlocked Nightmare mode. I was still in level ~50-60 gear - I think my highest level item was 67 and lowest was 34. I was hoping for a new 'wall' to be forced to re-think my build, tweak talents, grind some gear... anything? Nope. I sailed through the entire Nightmare campaign and Inferno campaign in one morning without a single death. I didn't equip a single piece of new gear or change my build in any way. The game isn't hard enough. It seems they just tested the first few hours with an incomplete build, decided the difficulty seemed ok and then applied a flat incremental curve to hp/damage of monsters for every level thereafter without considering once people have a somewhat coherent build that their dps/survivability would skyrocket far beyond the difficulty level of the mobs. The crutch is that they've got the infinitely scaling 'mythic rift' but I feel like it's lazily applied and I've just reached it far too soon. Is that all I've got now? I'm honestly surprised at just how cool this game is. I never really played an idle game outside of something silly like Stone Simulator, but this was is actually really nice. Pros: Gear System - The game is essentially "diablo" as a idle ARPG. You have multiple classes and the loot is addicting. Multiple paths to upgrade gear, farm materials and continue to see your character improve. Legendary items with special effects that make gear builds interesting and something you can build around a specific item effect. You have gems as well for extra stat upgrades on gear and weapons. Deep talent trees that make for fun builds to experiment with to see how far your character can keep going on it's own. Overall I really think its a cool game to let play and then come back and min/max your character before you let it idle again. Classes - The classes are super fun in the game. I personally have tried Warrior and Sorceror and so far I like both of them. There are even more classes to choose from so theres definitely something to have here for most people. Skill Trees - The skill trees are vast. Not only is there a ton of skills to choose from in your talent trees, that you will actually struggle to choose because alot of them are good, but you will also choose from life skills that require gold for permanent stats boosts and of course you have a paragon tree for endgame leveling. It's all here. Cons: Sound effects: some of the sound effects for weapons and skills are pretty bad. Whirlwind sounds terrible to be honest. I think they need to work on this to really make the classes sound better. I know most people idle play but still. Graphics - They leave a lot to be desired. Obviously its a smaller game, totally understand, but I was not feeling the graphics that much in the game. Even for someone who usually likes older style graphics too, theres just something off with this one. RMT Auction House - The game features a real money trading auction house, essentially turning this idle game into a money farming pit for some people. It would lead me to believe the game could potentially be designed in a way to try to force the use of this auction house, but so far I havent experienced that 40 levels in. Overall Deskrawl is a cool introduction for me to idle video games and its something nice to check on every now and then while it farms itself in the background. I enjoy it for what it is and its a cool addition to my library. Thanks for reading.

I want to preface that I do enjoy the game. I like idlers and am going to keep playing these but I am tentatively marking my review as negative due to reasons I'll explain below. I have a level 34 Sorc and a level 22 Hunter and I have 50/85 notes in the life skill tree unlocked and 6/12 of the features. I focused on mostly gold find, item find, and experience to try and make that progress speed feel better. The amount of experience you end up needing after 13~ just feel so excessive. Progression in general feels like it takes a noise dive after this point. At level 18~ the gear just stops dropping at regular consistency. Not to mention that when it does drop, get ready for the classic ARPG tropes of gear affixes like reduced damage take from poison or fire or damage to enemies far from you or damage increase to lightning when your class doesn't have a lightning ability to level 30+. There are a lot of useless affixes and I'm fine with that. The painful part about that is gear drops so infrequently that finally getting a rare piece of gear with Arcane damage reduction, thorns, and damage to vulnerable targets on my hunter when I can't apply vulnerability till level 30 just feels awful. The hunter, (after getting most of that life skill tree) did feel better up to 18~ but again it started to grind to a painful slow down in experience speed. This is with 105% increased experience from the life skill tree and with experience potions active. For reference, I have cleared the level 24 Kings Wood South 13 times on my hunter and earned 443k~ experience from those 13 clears. That is about a full level from mid 21 to mid 22. The clears are taking around 2~3 minutes. The scaling just feels off in terms of how much experience is required vs how much you get this early on in the play through. I get it is an Idle game, I have played quite a lot of them, but I tend to find more idles leaning into the grinding aspect as you progress further into the mid game and late game. There are still 2 more full on difficulties and 40 levels and honestly I can't even imagine how long it would be taking to get to that point. I enjoy the grind, but the fact that leveling up this early is taking this long and the gear also is already a pain and stopping my character from beating bosses in the lowest difficult almost scares me away from wanting to continue. I am going to keep playing because I do want to try out the other classes and I want to unlock more skills for more character customizations, but I still wanted to post feedback now. The games looks like it has a lot of content that I can enjoy, but I wish the scaling this early on in progress wasn't this horrible feeling. - End Game Edit - Drop rates are a pain but As I've continued to farm I've slowly got some blackmist items and the dev has clearly been listening to feedback. Love the changes to potions requiring more commonly farmed boss materials. They've even made it easier to farm Mythic rifts and obtain runes with the new transmutation system. I really appreciate how receptive the dev has been and how fast they have been reacting to community feedback and making the game better because of it. I've changed my recommendation to positive. I do believe the leveling experiencing for your first character is rough. Nothing in the early game has been adjusted so that will still be tough, but once you get your build clicking, I was able to finish basically all difficulties with a level 45 hunter. That does beg the question, was the scaling appropriate? Level 45 hunter with some good legendaries and rolled well yellows was able to go from hard stuck to clearing all difficulties. I kept coming back and enjoying the dopamine of coming back to more loot and level progression so I think it is only far to update me review.
